title: 22. Interview: Design YouTube
summary: Interview Q&A for Design YouTube — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Design YouTube interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Step 6: Trade-offs & Interview Q&A (5 min)
sections.body:
### Trade-offs Discussed
- **HLS vs DASH vs Progressive**: HLS is Apple-native, simplest, broadly supported; DASH is more flexible (lower latency with LL-DASH); progressive (MP4) is simplest but no adaptive bitrate. We pick HLS for compatibility, with DASH for low-latency live.
- **AV1 vs VP9 vs H.264**: AV1 gives 30% better compression than VP9 (50% better than H.264) but is 10× slower to encode. We pick H.264 for fast turnaround on new uploads, AV1 for popular videos (re-transcode overnight).
- **Per-segment vs per-variant transcoding**: per-segment (chunked encoding) reduces time-to-first-frame but adds complexity. Per-variant is simpler. We pick per-variant with parallel workers.
- **CDN hit ratio vs origin cost**: edge caching 95% means only 5% of bytes hit GCS ($0.09/GB egress). Pure origin would cost 20× more. Always-on CDN.
- **Two-tower ANN vs graph-based recs**: ANN is simpler, scales to billions of items. Graph-based (e.g., "users who watched X also watched Y") is more interpretable but expensive to compute. We pick ANN with graph features as inputs.
- **Counter accuracy vs throughput**: Cassandra counters are fast but lossy under contention. Batched Kafka increments (60 s windows) reduce drift to 99.9% accuracy. For view counts specifically, YouTube displays rounded numbers ("1.2M views") to avoid precision expectations.

### Conceptual Interview Questions

### Q1. Why does YouTube transcode every video into 12+ variants instead of just serving the original?
**Answer:** Three reasons. (1) **Adaptive bitrate streaming**: viewers have wildly different bandwidth (rural DSL at 1 Mbps, fiber at 1 Gbps, mobile at 5 Mbps). If we served only the original 4K upload, mobile users would buffer constantly. By generating 6 resolutions (240p–4K), the player picks the highest sustainable bitrate and adapts on the fly. (2) **Codec compatibility**: H.264 is universally supported but inefficient. VP9 and AV1 are 30–50% smaller but not supported on older devices. By generating all three, we serve AV1 to modern browsers (smaller bytes = lower CDN cost) and H.264 to old devices. (3) **Storage vs bandwidth trade-off**: storing 12 variants costs 12× storage but cuts bandwidth 2–4× (smaller files for low-bandwidth viewers, modern codecs for modern viewers). At YouTube's scale (50 PB/day egress), bandwidth dominates, so the trade-off favors more variants. Real-world: YouTube, Netflix, and Twitch all generate 5–12 variants per video; the exact set is tuned by region and device mix.
**Visual:**
```
Original upload (4K, H.264, 100 MB)
    |
    v
Transcoder farm -> 12 variants:
  240p × {h264, vp9, av1}     -- 3 MB, 1.5 MB, 1 MB
  360p × {h264, vp9, av1}     -- 6 MB, 3 MB, 2 MB
  ...
  4K   × {h264, vp9, av1}     -- 100 MB, 60 MB, 40 MB

Player picks best variant for bandwidth + codec support
Modern Chrome on fiber: 4K AV1 (40 MB)
Old iPhone on 3G: 240p H.264 (3 MB)
```

### Q2. How does HLS adaptive bitrate streaming actually work?
**Answer:** HLS (HTTP Live Streaming, Apple's protocol) works as follows. (1) The server segments each video variant into small chunks (10 s each) and stores them as `.ts` files with a `.m3u8` playlist per variant. (2) The server also publishes a `master.m3u8` playlist that lists all variants with their bitrates and resolutions. (3) The player fetches the master playlist, measures available bandwidth (typically by timing the first few segment downloads), and picks the highest sustainable variant. (4) As the player downloads each segment, it continuously re-evaluates bandwidth. If bandwidth drops (e.g., user moves to weaker WiFi), the player switches to a lower-bitrate variant for the next segment — seamlessly, because segments are independent. (5) If bandwidth improves, the player switches back up. (6) The player pre-fetches the next 2–3 segments to absorb brief bandwidth dips. Benefits: (a) buffering is minimized (player adapts within 2 s); (b) only the bytes actually needed are fetched (saves bandwidth); (c) segments are small and cache well at CDN edges (95%+ hit ratio). Trade-off: 10-s segments introduce 10-s latency for live streaming — LL-HLS (Low-Latency HLS) reduces this to 2 s.
**Visual:**
```
master.m3u8:
  #EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=400000,RESOLUTION=426x240
  240p/playlist.m3u8
  #EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=800000,RESOLUTION=640x360
  360p/playlist.m3u8
  ...
  #EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=17000000,RESOLUTION=3840x2160
  4K/playlist.m3u8

Player: measures bandwidth = 5 Mbps
  -> picks 720p variant
  -> fetches seg_0001.ts, seg_0002.ts, ...
  -> if bandwidth drops to 1 Mbps, next segment from 360p
  -> if bandwidth recovers, switch back to 720p
```

### Q3. How does YouTube's recommendation system work at a high level?
**Answer:** YouTube's recommender is a **two-stage retrieval + ranking** pipeline. **Stage 1 — Candidate generation**: instead of scanning all 100 M+ videos, we use **approximate nearest neighbor (ANN)** over video embeddings. Each video is embedded into a 256-dim vector by a neural network trained on co-watch signals (users who watched A also watched B) and content features (title, tags, thumbnail). Each user is embedded similarly based on watch history. At request time, the user embedding is queried against a FAISS index of all video embeddings to retrieve top 1 000 candidates in < 5 ms. **Stage 2 — Ranking**: a deep neural network scores each candidate on multiple objectives — predicted watch time, probability of like, probability of subscribe, probability of "not interested" (negative signal). The final score is a weighted combination. The top 20 are returned, with diversity constraints (max 3 from same channel, max 5 from same topic). The model is retrained daily on the previous day's watch data. Trade-off: a richer model gives better recs but adds latency. We pick a fast candidate generator (ANN, 5 ms) + a moderate-depth ranker (50 ms) with strict timeouts. Real-world: YouTube's "Up Next" uses this architecture (described in their 2016 paper "Deep Neural Networks for YouTube Recommendations").
**Visual:**
```
User request: GET /recommendations
  |
  v
Stage 1: Candidate generation (5 ms)
  user embedding (from Redis) -> FAISS ANN over 100M video embeddings
  -> top 1000 candidates
  -> filter: already watched, region-blocked, age-restricted
  |
  v
Stage 2: Ranking (50 ms)
  deep NN: predicts P(watch_time), P(like), P(subscribe), P(not_interested)
  weighted combination -> score per candidate
  |
  v
Diversity: max 3 per channel, max 5 per topic
  |
  v
Top 20 -> return to client
```

### Q4. How does YouTube handle a new viral video that gets 100 M views in 24 hours?
**Answer:** Five defenses. (1) **CDN edge caching**: as soon as a segment is requested from a POP, it's cached for 24 h. With 100 M views across 200 POPs, each POP serves ~500 k views — all cache hits after the first request per segment. (2) **Origin shield**: a regional cache tier protects GCS from thundering herds. If 100 POPs miss simultaneously (e.g., a new viral segment), they all hit the origin shield (one cache) instead of GCS directly. The shield fetches from GCS once and serves all 100 POPs. (3) **Pre-warming**: for videos that show early viral signals (high view velocity in first hour), a job pre-fetches the first 5 segments to all POPs before viewers arrive. (4) **Adaptive bitrate popularity**: the player reports which bitrates are watched; we transcode-on-demand for rare bitrates (e.g., 8K) only when first requested. (5) **Load shedding**: if a POP saturates, it serves lower-bitrate variants (smaller segments, less CPU) and degrades gracefully. Real-world: YouTube handled "Gangnam Style" (1 B views in 5 months, 2012) and "Baby Shark" (10 B views, 2020) without visible degradation using exactly this.
**Visual:**
```
Viral video drops (100M views in 24h)
  |
  +--> CDN edge: 200 POPs, each caches segments (24h TTL)
  |     -> 99%+ hit ratio after first request per POP per segment
  |
  +--> Origin shield: regional cache protects GCS
  |     -> if 100 POPs miss, shield fetches from GCS once
  |
  +--> Pre-warming: viral signal -> fetch first 5 segments to all POPs
  |
  +--> Adaptive bitrate: rare variants (8K) transcoded on-demand
  |
  +--> Load shedding: saturated POP -> serve lower-bitrate variants
```

### Q5. How does YouTube handle the upload of a 100 GB video without timing out?
**Answer:** Resumable, parallel, chunked uploads. (1) **Presigned URL**: the client calls `POST /upload/start` to get a presigned GCS URL and a `video_id`. The URL allows the client to upload bytes **directly to GCS**, bypassing our API servers — this avoids saturating our bandwidth and lets GCS handle the heavy lifting. (2) **Chunked**: the client splits the file into 8 MB chunks (Google's recommended size). Each chunk is a separate HTTP PUT with a `Content-Range` header indicating which bytes. GCS acknowledges each chunk independently. (3) **Parallel**: 8 chunks upload in parallel, saturating the available bandwidth. (4) **Resumable**: if the connection drops mid-upload, the client queries GCS with `Content-Range: bytes */{file_size}` (asterisk = "tell me what you have"). GCS responds with `308 Resume Incomplete` and a `Range` header indicating which bytes are already stored. The client resumes from there. (5) **Idempotent**: each chunk PUT is idempotent (re-uploading a chunk GCS already has is a no-op). (6) **Final commit**: after the last chunk, GCS assembles the object and the client calls `POST /videos/{id}` to finalize. Real-world: Google Drive, YouTube, and S3 multipart uploads all use this pattern.
**Visual:**
```
1. POST /upload/start -> presigned GCS URL + video_id
2. Split file into 8MB chunks
3. Parallel PUT chunks:
   PUT chunk 0: Content-Range: bytes 0-8388607/100GB
   PUT chunk 1: Content-Range: bytes 8388608-16777215/100GB
   ... (8 in parallel)
4. Connection drops:
   HEAD with Content-Range: bytes */100GB
   -> 308 Resume Incomplete, Range: bytes 0-536870911
   -> resume from chunk 64
5. Final PUT -> 200 OK
6. POST /videos/{id} -> finalize metadata
```

### Q6. How does YouTube track watch time accurately for 5 B views/day?
**Answer:** Watch-time tracking is critical — it drives recommendations, creator payouts, and analytics. (1) **Client telemetry**: the player sends a `watch_10s` event every 10 seconds of playback (not wall-clock — actual playback time, so pausing or seeking doesn't inflate it). Plus `play`, `pause`, `seek`, `complete` events. (2) **Firehose**: 5 B views/day × 30 events/view = 150 B events/day = ~1.7 M events/s. Kafka absorbs this with partitioning by `video_id` (so events for the same video land on the same consumer). (3) **Aggregation**: Flink jobs aggregate per (video_id, hour) — total watch time, unique viewers, average completion rate. Output written to Cassandra for low-latency reads and to BigQuery for analytics. (4) **Deduplication**: events have client-generated UUIDs; Flink deduplicates within a 5-min window (in case of retries). (5) **Bot filtering**: ML model scores each session for bot probability; suspicious events are flagged and excluded from official counts. (6) **Reconciliation**: a nightly job recomputes authoritative view counts from the deduped event log and updates Spanner. Displayed counts are rounded ("1.2M views") to avoid precision expectations. Real-world: YouTube has acknowledged that view counts can lag by hours for viral videos and are revised as bot filtering runs.
**Visual:**
```
Player -> every 10s playback -> POST /events {type:watch_10s, position:60}
                                    |
                                    v
                                 Kafka (1.7M events/s, partitioned by video_id)
                                    |
                                    v
                                 Flink aggregator
                                    |
                  +-----------------+-----------------+
                  |                                   |
                  v                                   v
              Cassandra                          BigQuery
              (per video/hour,                   (analytics,
               low-latency)                       creator dashboard)

Nightly reconciliation: authoritative view counts -> Spanner
Displayed: "1.2M views" (rounded)
```

### Q7. How does YouTube handle live streaming differently from VOD?
**Answer:** Live streaming is fundamentally different from VOD. (1) **Ingest**: streamer's app pushes RTMP/SRT to a regional ingest endpoint. Latency to ingest must be < 200 ms. (2) **Real-time transcoding**: a transcoder (FFmpeg with NVENC, or AWS IVS/MediaLive) generates multiple bitrates simultaneously in real time (1× speed — must keep up). Unlike VOD where we can spend 10× realtime encoding, live is bounded by realtime. (3) **Packaging**: LL-HLS (Low-Latency HLS) segments, 2 s each (vs 10 s for VOD). Published to CDN as they're produced. (4) **CDN**: low-latency CDN config (CloudFront LL-HLS, Akamai Limelight). Viewers fetch segments as they're published. End-to-end latency: 3–10 s (vs instant for VOD). (5) **Fanout**: when streamer goes live, publish a notification to subscribers (like a new video but with a "live" badge). Viewer count tracked in Redis (INCR on join, DECR on leave). (6) **Live chat**: separate WebSocket service (millions of concurrent connections) for real-time comments. (7) **Recording**: when streamer ends, the recording is processed through the normal VOD pipeline (transcode to all variants, publish as a regular video). Trade-off: live transcoding is expensive ($0.50–2/hour per stream); limit free users to 12 h, charge pro users. Real-world: YouTube Live, Twitch, and Facebook Live all use this architecture.
**Visual:**
```
VOD:
  upload (slow, 100s of MB) -> transcode (10x realtime, 12 variants)
  -> segment (10s chunks) -> CDN -> viewer (instant, cached)

Live:
  streamer -> RTMP -> ingest (regional)
  -> real-time transcoder (1x realtime, 4-6 variants)
  -> LL-HLS packager (2s segments)
  -> CDN edge -> viewers (3-10s latency)
  Live chat: WebSocket -> millions of concurrent connections
  On end: save recording -> normal VOD pipeline
```

### Scenario-Based Interview Questions

### Q1. A user reports the video keeps buffering on their fiber connection. How do you debug?
**Answer:** Step-by-step. (1) **Confirm the user's bandwidth**: ask them to run a speed test. "Fiber" can mean 100 Mbps or 1 Gbps; if their router is throttling or their ISP has a peering issue with Google, effective bandwidth may be lower. (2) **Check the player's reported bitrate**: most players (YouTube's HTML5 player) expose diagnostics (right-click → Stats for Nerds). What's the current `Network Activity` and `Buffer Health`? If buffer is consistently < 1 s, the player can't keep up. (3) **Which variant is the player on?** If the player is stuck on 240p despite fiber, the ABR algorithm may be misreporting bandwidth — possibly a client bug after a recent player update. (4) **CDN edge health**: is the user's nearest POP healthy? Check CDN dashboards for that region — is the POP saturated or degraded? (5) **Specific video or all videos?** If only one video buffers, that video's segments may be missing from the user's POP (cold cache). Try a different video — if it plays fine, the issue is content placement. (6) **ISP peering**: if the user's ISP has a congested peering link to Google, latency spikes will cause buffering. Tools like M-Lab can measure this. (7) **Time of day**: peak evening hours may saturate the user's local node — not YouTube's fault. Most likely cause: either a player ABR bug (try refresh/reinstall) or ISP peering congestion (escalate to Google's network team).
**Visual:**
```
Buffering reported on fiber
  |
  +--> Speed test: actual bandwidth?
  +--> Player Stats for Nerds: buffer health, current bitrate
  +--> Stuck on low bitrate? -> ABR bug, client issue
  +--> CDN POP healthy? -> check regional dashboard
  +--> Specific video? -> cold cache, content placement
  +--> ISP peering congested? -> M-Lab measurement
  +--> Peak evening? -> local node saturation
```

### Q2. The CEO wants to add 4K live streaming. How does the architecture change?
**Answer:** 4K live is significantly harder than 1080p live. (1) **Encoder cost**: 4K encoding is ~4× the CPU of 1080p. Real-time 4K encoding requires hardware acceleration (NVENC NVENC HEVC, or dedicated ASICs like Netint). Transcoder farm must scale up. (2) **Bandwidth**: 4K live at 20 Mbps per stream × 100 k concurrent viewers = 2 Tbps egress — only CDN can handle this. Pre-warm edge caches aggressively. (3) **Ingest**: streamer needs ≥ 25 Mbps upload (most home fiber supports this, but mobile doesn't). Limit 4K live to verified channels. (4) **Codec**: H.265 (HEVC) or AV1 — H.264 4K at 25 Mbps is wasteful. HEVC cuts it to 15 Mbps; AV1 to 10 Mbps. But HEVC has licensing issues; AV1 is slow to encode in realtime. (5) **LL-HLS**: keep 2-s segments; the player fetches 4K segments when bandwidth allows, falls back to 1080p otherwise. (6) **DRM**: 4K content typically requires Widevine L1 (hardware DRM) — most browsers don't support 4K without it. (7) **Recording**: on end, transcode the 4K recording to all standard VOD variants (240p–4K). (8) **Cost recovery**: 4K live is expensive — charge creators a premium or limit to Partner Program members. Real-world: YouTube and Twitch both gate 4K live behind partner status.
**Visual:**
```
4K live streamer:
  Encoder: NVENC HEVC or AV1 ASIC (1x realtime, 4x CPU of 1080p)
  Ingest: requires 25 Mbps upload (verified channels only)
  Codec: HEVC (15 Mbps) or AV1 (10 Mbps)
  CDN: pre-warm edges, 2 Tbps egress potential
  DRM: Widevine L1 (hardware) for 4K
  Player: LL-HLS 2s segments, ABR fallback to 1080p
  Cost: gate behind Partner Program
```

### Q3. A creator uploads a 10-hour 4K video and the transcoder is taking 12 hours. How do you speed it up?
**Answer:** Several optimizations. (1) **Chunked transcoding**: instead of transcoding the whole video sequentially, split it into 10-min chunks and transcode each chunk in parallel on different workers. 10 h video / 10 min chunks = 60 chunks × 12 variants = 720 parallel jobs. With 100 workers, that's ~7 batches → 1–2 h total instead of 12 h. (2) **Hardware acceleration**: ensure NVENC (NVIDIA) or QSV (Intel) is enabled — 5–10× faster than CPU encoding. (3) **Codec priority**: encode H.264 first (fastest, broadly compatible) so the video can be published; re-encode to VP9/AV1 in the background overnight. (4) **Skip rare variants**: don't encode 8K unless requested; don't encode AV1 for low resolutions (the savings are tiny). (5) **Two-pass vs one-pass**: switch to one-pass for the initial publish; do a two-pass re-encode overnight for higher quality. (6) **Pre-emptive scaling**: auto-scale the transcoder farm based on upload volume; keep spare capacity for spikes. (7) **Communicate to creator**: show "Processing: 60% complete, HD available now, 4K available in 4 hours." YouTube does exactly this — different resolutions become available at different times. Real-world: YouTube's processing pipeline publishes the lowest-resolution variant first (often within minutes), then progressively higher resolutions.
**Visual:**
```
10h 4K upload -> 12h transcode (sequential)
  |
  +--> Chunked: split into 60 x 10min chunks
  |     60 chunks x 12 variants = 720 parallel jobs
  |     100 workers -> 7 batches -> 1-2h total
  |
  +--> Hardware: NVENC/QSV (5-10x faster than CPU)
  +--> Priority: H.264 first (publish immediately)
  |                VP9/AV1 overnight
  +--> Skip: 8K (rare), AV1 at low res (savings tiny)
  +--> Show creator: "HD available now, 4K in 4h"
```

### Q4. A viral video has 50 M views in 24 hours and the view counter shows wrong numbers. What happened?
**Answer:** Three likely causes. (1) **Bot filtering lag**: YouTube's bot detection runs continuously but final counts are reconciled nightly. During a viral spike, the live counter may include bot views that are later removed. By morning, the count may drop (a known phenomenon — "YouTube deleted my views!"). (2) **Flink aggregation lag**: at 1.7 M events/s for a viral video, the Flink aggregator may lag by minutes to hours. The displayed count is from a 5-min-old snapshot. (3) **CDN caching of count**: the view count is cached at the CDN edge for 60 s; during a viral spike, the displayed count lags by up to 60 s × the number of POPs the user bounces between. (4) **Deduplication**: if a user watches the video 10 times in a row, only 1 view counts (after the 30-s threshold). If dedup is broken, counts inflate. (5) **Display rounding**: "50M views" might actually be 49.7 M or 50.3 M — YouTube rounds to 2 significant figures. Fix: wait for the nightly reconciliation, check Flink job health, verify dedup logic, and communicate to the creator that counts are approximate during viral spikes. Real-world: YouTube explicitly states that view counts during viral spikes are provisional and may be adjusted.
**Visual:**
```
50M views in 24h, counter wrong
  |
  +--> Bot filtering lag? -> nightly reconciliation will adjust
  +--> Flink aggregation lag? -> check job health, consumer lag
  +--> CDN count cache stale? -> 60s TTL, refreshes
  +--> Dedup broken? -> check 30s threshold logic
  +--> Display rounding? -> "50M" = 49.7M to 50.3M
  |
  Fix: wait for nightly reconciliation, verify Flink/dedup,
       communicate "counts are provisional during viral spikes"
```

### Q5. A creator reports their subscribers aren't getting notified of new uploads. How do you debug?
**Answer:** Step-by-step. (1) **Is the video actually published?** Check Spanner for the `video_id` — is `status = 'ready'` and `privacy = 'public'`? If `status = 'processing'`, the transcoder hasn't finished. If `privacy = 'private'`, no notifications are sent. (2) **Did the notification fire?** Check the notification service logs for the `video-ready` event — was it consumed? Were push notifications sent to APNS/FCM? (3) **Subscriber bell state**: YouTube has a "bell" icon (all notifications) vs default (some notifications). If subscribers haven't toggled the bell, they get notifications only for some uploads (algorithmic). Check the subscriber's bell state. (4) **Notification rate limiting**: YouTube caps notifications per user per day. If the subscriber has hit the cap (e.g., 100 channels all posted today), the new notification is dropped. (5) **APNS/FCM delivery**: the push service may have failed to deliver (token expired, app uninstalled). Check delivery receipts. (6) **Email digest**: if the subscriber is on email digest, notifications are batched (daily/weekly) — they'd see it tomorrow. (7) **Test with the creator**: have the creator manually check a known subscriber's account — do they see the video on their home page (subscription feed)? Most likely cause: subscribers haven't enabled the bell, or they have hit the daily notification cap. Fix: educate creators to ask subscribers to ring the bell.
**Visual:**
```
Subscribers not getting notified
  |
  +--> Video published? status=ready, privacy=public?
  +--> Notification fired? -> check notif service logs
  +--> Bell state? -> default = some; bell = all
  +--> Rate limit hit? -> 100/day cap, drop new notifs
  +--> APNS/FCM delivered? -> check receipts, token validity
  +--> Email digest? -> batched, see tomorrow
  +--> Subscription feed? -> check if video appears there
  |
  Most likely: bell not enabled, or daily cap hit
```

### Q6. The CDN cost is exploding — $50 M/month and growing. How do you reduce it?
**Answer:** Multi-pronged. (1) **AV1 for popular videos**: re-transcode the top 10 k most-watched videos to AV1 (30–50% smaller than H.264). Saves ~30% on those videos' egress. (2) **Lower default bitrate**: serve 720p as the default instead of 1080p (user can manually bump to 1080p). Saves 50% on default views. (3) **Pre-fetch less aggressively**: pre-fetch next 1 segment instead of 3 — saves bandwidth on users who abandon. (4) **Tiered CDN**: use Google Global Cache (cheaper, owned) for tier-1, Akamai (expensive, third-party) for tier-2 overflow. Route more traffic to GGC. (5) **Longer TTL at edge**: increase HLS segment cache TTL from 24 h to 7 days — most views happen in the first week, so 7-day TTL captures them. (6) **Peer caching with ISPs**: partner with major ISPs to place cache appliances in their data centers (Netflix Open Connect model). Free for the ISP; cheap for us. (7) **Lower-bitrate mobile**: serve 360p to mobile by default (most phones have small screens where 720p is wasted). (8) **Vary by region**: in regions with cheap bandwidth (US, EU), serve higher bitrate; in expensive regions (developing countries), serve lower. (9) **Audit**: ensure no orphaned segments (deleted video but segments still cached). Real-world: YouTube, Netflix, and Facebook all invest heavily in CDN cost optimization; AV1 adoption is the biggest lever.
**Visual:**
```
$50M/month CDN cost
  |
  +--> AV1 for top 10k videos (-30% on those)
  +--> Default 720p instead of 1080p (-50% on default views)
  +--> Pre-fetch 1 segment not 3 (-30% on abandoners)
  +--> More GGC, less Akamai (-50% on overflow)
  +--> Cache TTL 24h -> 7d (more hits)
  +--> ISP peer caching appliances (free for ISP)
  +--> Mobile: 360p default
  +--> Region-tiered bitrate
  -> 50% cost reduction in 6 months
```

### Q7. A user uploads a video that contains copyrighted music. How does Content ID work at scale?
**Answer:** Content ID is YouTube's copyright system. (1) **Reference library**: copyright holders upload reference files (their songs, movies) to YouTube. YouTube computes an audio fingerprint (a compact hash of the audio's spectral features) and stores it in a massive index. (2) **Upload scan**: when a creator uploads a video, the transcoder computes the same audio fingerprint and queries the index. (3) **Match detection**: if the fingerprint matches a reference (with > X% similarity and > Y seconds duration), it's a match. The system can identify matches even with pitch shifts, time stretching, or background noise — the fingerprint is robust to these. (4) **Action policy**: the copyright holder pre-configures an action — monetize (run ads, give revenue to the holder), block (in some regions), or track (just analytics). The action is applied automatically. (5) **Dispute**: the creator can dispute (e.g., "fair use"). The holder reviews and either releases the claim or upholds it. (6) **Scale**: the reference library has 100 M+ files. Fingerprint matching is O(1) per query thanks to the index. (7) **Visual Content ID**: same approach for video (a perceptual hash of keyframes). Trade-off: false positives (a 5-second sample triggers a claim) annoy creators; false negatives (copyrighted material not detected) annoy holders. YouTube tunes the thresholds continuously. Real-world: Content ID has paid out billions to copyright holders since 2007.
**Visual:**
```
Copyright holder -> upload reference -> audio fingerprint -> index (100M+ files)

Creator uploads video:
  transcoder -> audio fingerprint -> query index
  -> match? (similarity > X%, duration > Y seconds)
     |
     +--> No match -> publish normally
     +--> Match -> apply holder's policy:
             - Monetize (ads -> revenue to holder)
             - Block (region-specific)
             - Track (analytics only)
     +--> Creator disputes -> holder reviews -> release or uphold
```

quiz.question: How does YouTube's recommendation system work at a high level?
options: Watch-time tracking is critical — it drives recommendations, creator payouts, and analytics.
4K live is significantly harder than 1080p live. (1) Encoder cost: 4K encoding is ~4× the CPU of 1080p.
Several optimizations. (1) Chunked transcoding: instead of transcoding the whole video sequentially, split it into 10-min chunks and transcode each chunk in parallel on different workers.
YouTube's recommender is a two-stage retrieval + ranking pipeline.
quiz.explanation: YouTube's recommender is a two-stage retrieval + ranking pipeline. Stage 1 — Candidate generation: instead of scanning all 100 M+ videos, we use approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) over video embeddings. Each video is embedded into a 256-dim vector by a neural network trained on co-watch signals (users who watched A also watched B) and content features (title, tags, thumbnail).

quiz.explanation: Five defenses. (1) CDN edge caching: as soon as a segment is requested from a POP, it's cached for 24 h. With 100 M views across 200 POPs, each POP serves ~500 k views — all cache hits after the first request per segment.

quiz.explanation: Resumable, parallel, chunked uploads. (1) Presigned URL: the client calls POST /upload/start to get a presigned GCS URL and a video_id.
